summary.title: Falsehoods Junior Developers believe about becoming Senior
summary.one_liner: Junior developers often expect seniority to bring omniscience, glamorous work and free time, but the reality is comfort with uncertainty, boring-but-vital work, boundary management and adaptability.
keywords: saying i don't know at work
skills that make a senior engineer
takeaways: Seniority is less about knowing all answers and more about staying calm and knowing how to find answers quickly.
Senior work includes legacy maintenance, documentation, reviews and meetings, not only the interesting tickets.
Big technical changes must be pitched in terms of cost, risk, upside and fallback, since business priorities drive decisions.
Seniors have autonomy over their calendar, so boundary management matters more than raw hours.
Job security comes from adaptability and a network outside your current team, not from being the only expert on one legacy system.
summary.summary: A personal essay by Vadim Kravchenko, framed as a list of expectation-versus-reality pairs about becoming a senior developer. Each section covers a myth (such as knowing every answer, working only on the latest tech, avoiding boring tasks, rewriting systems quickly, having free time, or being irreplaceable) and contrasts it with lived experience. The piece is anecdotal and opinion-based rather than a tutorial, and it includes a few concrete examples like an anecdote about a senior engineer admitting he had no clue during a broken fstab incident. The page also includes reader comments and promotional content, which are not part of the core advice.
